questions.text: 99% train accuracy, 72% test. Walk me through what you do.
points: Name it as a variance problem before touching anything — then check it isn't leakage inverted
Cheapest first: more data · stronger regularisation · fewer features · simpler model
Learning curve tells you which — converging gap = more data helps, flat gap = it won't
Verify the split is honest (grouping, time order) before blaming the model
Cross-validate the fix; a single held-out set will happily lie to you twice
questions.badge: Evergreen — the single most-asked ML interview question, in scenario form.
questions.flow: name variance → check the split → learning curve → regularise or add data → re-CV
questions.trap: jumping straight to hyperparameter tuning

drill.prompt: from jbtiq_ml Q1: "Your model gets 99% train accuracy and 72% test accuracy. Walk me through what you do."
drill.badge: Evergreen — the single most-asked ML interview question, in scenario form.
drill.hint: Don't jump to a fix. What do you have to rule out before you accept "overfitting" as the diagnosis?
points: First rule out that the gap is real: is the test set drawn from the same distribution, is it big enough for 72% to be meaningful (confidence interval), and is there leakage in train that inflates the 99%? A leaked ID or target-derived feature looks exactly like this.

If real, it's high variance: model capacity exceeds what the data supports. Confirm with a learning curve — if train and validation converge as data grows, you're data-hungry; if the gap persists flat, it's capacity/regularization.

Fix ladder, cheapest first: more/better data or augmentation → stronger regularization (L1/L2, dropout, tree depth/min_samples_leaf, early stopping) → simpler model or fewer features → ensembling/bagging to average variance away.
Say the diagnostic discipline: one change at a time, measured on a held-out set you don't tune on, and use CV rather than a single split so you're not chasing split noise.
Senior addition: check whether 72% is actually bad for the task — compare against a baseline (majority class, simple heuristic, human) before optimising anything.
drill.oneLiner: First I'd rule out leakage and test-set noise, then read a learning curve to tell data hunger from excess capacity — and only then pick between more data and more regularization.
drill.followUp: "The learning curve is flat and you can't get more data." → reduce capacity, regularize harder, engineer better features, or accept and calibrate expectations.

questions.text: CV score 0.94, production 0.71. Nothing in the code changed. Where do you look first?
points: Leakage is the first hypothesis, not drift — drift takes time, this gap was there on day one
Target leakage: a feature computed after the label event exists
Split leakage: same entity in train and test, or future rows leaking backward in time
Preprocessing leakage: scaler/encoder/imputer fit on the full dataset before splitting
Then check train–serve skew — different code paths computing "the same" feature
questions.badge: Trending — recurs constantly on LeetCode Discuss ML threads + LinkedIn "why my model failed" posts (2025–26)
questions.flow: leakage first (target → split → preprocessing) → then skew → drift last
questions.trap: calling it drift on day one — drift doesn't arrive pre-installed

drill.prompt: from jbtiq_ml Q6: "Your CV score is 0.94 and production is 0.71. Nothing about the code changed. Where do you look first?"
drill.badge: Trending — recurs constantly on LeetCode Discuss ML threads + LinkedIn "why my model failed" posts (2025–26)
drill.hint: There are only a few ways an offline number can be optimistic. Name the leakage families before you name drift.
points: Leakage first, drift second — leakage is the more common cause of a gap this large. Families: (1) target leakage (a feature computed from or after the outcome — refund flag, "days since cancellation"); (2) train/test contamination (fitting the scaler/imputer/encoder on the full dataset before splitting, duplicate rows, near-duplicates); (3) temporal leakage (random split on time-ordered data → training on the future); (4) group leakage (same user/device across folds).

Then train-serve skew: features computed differently in the training pipeline vs the serving path — different defaults for missing values, different time zones, different aggregation windows, a feature that's available in the warehouse but not at request time.

Then genuine distribution shift: covariate shift, label shift, or concept drift. Diagnose by scoring the production feature distributions against training (PSI/KS per feature) and by replaying production inputs through the offline pipeline.

Structural fixes: put every transform inside a Pipeline/ColumnTransformer fitted inside each CV fold, use GroupKFold or time-series CV where relevant, and share one feature-computation implementation between training and serving (a feature store exists for exactly this).
Say the audit trick: sort features by importance and ask of the top three, "would I know this at prediction time?" — that catches most target leakage in minutes.
drill.oneLiner: A gap that big is usually leakage or train-serve skew, not drift — so I audit the top features for availability at prediction time, check that every transform was fitted inside the fold, and replay production inputs through the offline pipeline.
drill.followUp: "How would you have caught it before shipping?" → time-based holdout, a leakage checklist in review, and shadow-scoring production traffic.

questions.text: Decompose bias-variance — and tell me where the classical picture is misleading.
points: Error = bias² + variance + irreducible noise; bias = wrong assumptions, variance = sensitivity to the sample
Classical U-curve says complexity past a point always hurts — modern over-parameterised models contradict it
Double descent: past the interpolation threshold, test error falls again
Operationally it's still the right diagnostic: gap between train and val is your variance read
Regularisation, ensembling and more data each attack a different term
questions.badge: Trending — the "where it's misleading" half recurs on LeetCode Discuss ML threads + LinkedIn posts since deep-learning-era interviews (2025–26)
questions.flow: decompose → diagnose from the train/val gap → attack the dominant term
questions.trap: reciting the U-curve as universal law in 2026

drill.prompt: from jbtiq_ml Q2: "Decompose the bias-variance tradeoff for me — and tell me where the classical picture is misleading."
drill.badge: Trending — the "where it's misleading" half recurs on LeetCode Discuss ML threads + LinkedIn posts since deep-learning-era interviews (2025–26)
drill.hint: Three terms in the decomposition, not two. Then: what does the U-shaped test-error curve look like for a hugely overparameterized model?
points: Expected squared error = bias² + variance + irreducible noise. Bias = systematic error from wrong assumptions (underfit); variance = sensitivity to the particular training sample (overfit); noise is the floor you cannot beat.
Classical picture: capacity ↑ → bias ↓, variance ↑ → U-shaped test error, pick the minimum. That still governs most tabular/classical ML, which is why it's the right first answer.

Where it misleads: double descent — past the interpolation threshold, test error can fall again for heavily overparameterized models. So "more parameters always overfits" is false for modern nets, and the tradeoff is better framed as effective capacity (architecture + regularization + optimization + data) than parameter count.
Also: the decomposition is exact for squared loss; for 0–1 loss it's only an analogy — worth saying, it signals you've read past the tutorial.
Practical use: bias and variance have different fixes, so the value of the framework is diagnostic — learning curves tell you which one you have.
drill.oneLiner: Bias², variance and irreducible noise — capacity trades the first two, but with modern overparameterized models double descent breaks the simple U-curve, so I reason about effective capacity, not parameter count.

questions.text: How do you split data when the same users appear many times and behaviour is seasonal?
points: Two independent violations: entity overlap and temporal order — fix both or the score is fiction
Entity → GroupKFold on user id, never plain stratified
Time → walk-forward / expanding window; test is always after train
Combine: group-aware split within a time-ordered fold
Seasonality means the test window must cover a comparable season, or you're measuring the calendar

drill.prompt: from jbtiq_ml Q7: "How do you split data for a model that predicts subscription cancellation, where users appear many times and behaviour changes seasonally?"
drill.badge: Trending — recurs on LeetCode Discuss + ML-Engineer JDs (2025–26)
drill.hint: Two independent leakage risks are named in the question. A single splitting strategy has to defeat both.
points: Two risks: entity leakage (the same user in train and test lets the model memorise the user, not the behaviour) and temporal leakage (seasonality means a random split trains on the future).

Correct construction: split by time first (train on ≤ T, validate on (T, T+Δ], test on the most recent window), and enforce group disjointness by user within that — i.e. a grouped, time-ordered split, validated with walk-forward CV across several time origins rather than a single cut.

Respect the prediction horizon and label delay: features may only use data up to the prediction timestamp, and the label window must be fully observed — otherwise the most recent rows are censored and look artificially clean.
Report the metric per time slice, not just pooled — a model that degrades monotonically over the test window is telling you the retraining cadence you need.

Say the final validation: the offline evaluation should mimic deployment exactly — train on the past, predict forward, no user overlap. If your CV doesn't look like production, its number is decoration.
drill.oneLiner: Time-ordered split with user-level group disjointness, validated walk-forward across multiple origins, with features truncated at the prediction timestamp and the label window fully observed.

questions.text: You used 5-fold CV to tune hyperparameters and reported that same CV score. What's wrong?
points: The score is optimistically biased — the folds were used to select, so they're no longer held out
Selecting over many candidates is fitting to fold noise; the more candidates, the worse the bias
Fix: nested CV — inner loop selects, outer loop estimates; or a untouched final hold-out
Nested costs k_outer × k_inner × candidates — pay it when the decision is expensive, not always
Cheap alternative: one clean hold-out set touched exactly once
questions.badge: Evergreen — the nested-CV question, in the form it's actually asked.
questions.flow: selection ≠ estimation → inner loop selects, outer estimates → or one untouched hold-out
questions.trap: treating the best CV score as the expected production score

drill.prompt: from jbtiq_ml Q34: "You used 5-fold CV to pick hyperparameters and reported that same CV score as the model's performance. What's wrong, and what's the fix?"
drill.badge: Evergreen — the nested-CV question, in the form it's actually asked.
drill.hint: The score did double duty. What does selecting-on-a-number do to that number as an estimate?
points: The CV score was used to select among many configurations, so the winner's score is optimistically biased — you picked the config that got luckiest on those folds (winner's curse / multiple comparisons). The more configs you tried, the bigger the inflation.

Fixes, by budget: hold out an untouched test set evaluated exactly once after all selection; or nested CV — inner loop tunes, outer loop estimates generalization of the whole procedure — when data is too scarce for a clean holdout.
Same discipline applies to everything that saw the folds: feature selection, encoder choices, threshold tuning. Anything selected on validation data contaminates it as an estimate.
Comparing two models honestly: differences within CV noise are not wins — use repeated CV with confidence intervals, or McNemar's / 5×2-CV paired tests when the decision matters.
Practical calibration to voice: the bias is small when you tried three configs and large when Optuna tried three hundred — the risk scales with search intensity.
drill.oneLiner: Selecting on a score biases that score upward — the winner got lucky on those folds — so I report from an untouched holdout or nested CV, and I treat within-noise differences as ties, not wins.

questions.text: How do you turn 'reduce churn' into an ML problem — and when do you say don't use ML?
points: Force the decision out first: who gets what intervention, when, at what cost?
Then the label: churn by when, and what counts — pauses, downgrades?
Then horizon and unit of prediction — per user per month is a choice, not a given
Metric follows the decision: cost of FP vs FN, plus the capacity constraint
Don't use ML when: no label, no feedback loop, rules work, or the action is fixed anyway
questions.badge: Trending — recurs on ML-Engineer/Architect JDs and LinkedIn interview write-ups (2025–26)
questions.flow: decision → label + horizon → metric from cost of error → is there a cheaper rule?
questions.trap: accepting "predict churn" as a spec

drill.prompt: from jbtiq_ml Q3: "How do you frame a vague business ask — 'reduce churn' — as an ML problem? And when do you tell them not to use ML?"
drill.badge: Trending — recurs on ML-Engineer/Architect JDs and LinkedIn interview write-ups (2025–26)
drill.hint: Four things must be nailed down before any model exists. And the "don't use ML" answer needs a concrete condition, not modesty.
points: Nail down, in order: the decision the model will change (who gets what intervention), the prediction target and its horizon (churn = no activity in 30 days? cancellation event?), the unit of prediction (user, account, session), and the cost matrix — what a false positive and a false negative each cost in currency.

Then define the label generation path: is the label available historically, is it observable at serving time without leakage, and what's the label delay (you can't know 30-day churn for last week's users).
Establish a baseline and a success threshold before modelling: majority class, a business rule, the current process. If a rule gets 90% of the value, ship the rule.

Say "don't use ML" when: the rule is expressible and stable, labels don't exist or are hopelessly noisy, the required accuracy is unachievable given noise, the cost of an error is unbounded (safety/legal) without a human in the loop, or the data drifts faster than you can retrain.
Architect framing: also decide online vs batch, latency budget, and how the prediction is acted on — an unusable prediction is a failed project regardless of AUC.
drill.oneLiner: Pin the decision, the target and horizon, the unit, and the cost of each error type — then compare against a rule-based baseline, and if the rule captures most of the value, ship the rule.

questions.text: ROC-AUC is 0.92 and the business says the model is useless. Reconcile.
points: ROC-AUC is prevalence-insensitive — it flatters models on rare positives
At 0.5% prevalence, a great ROC still means most flagged cases are false positives
Use PR-AUC and precision@k — the business only ever sees the top of the ranked list
AUC is threshold-free; the product ships a threshold, chosen from the cost of error
Ranking quality and operating-point quality are different claims — say which one you're making
questions.badge: Trending — recurs on LeetCode Discuss + LinkedIn ML posts (2025–26)
questions.flow: check prevalence → switch to PR-AUC / precision@k → pick the threshold from cost
questions.trap: defending the model with the metric instead of the decision

drill.prompt: from jbtiq_ml Q24: "ROC-AUC says 0.92, the business says the model is useless. Reconcile."
drill.badge: Trending — recurs on LeetCode Discuss + LinkedIn ML posts (2025–26)
drill.hint: What population does ROC average over, and what slice of it does the business actually operate in?
points: ROC-AUC is threshold-free and prevalence-insensitive: it averages ranking quality over all thresholds and both classes. Under heavy class imbalance, the FPR denominator is the huge negative class, so a model can flood the alert queue with false positives while ROC looks great.

The business lives at one operating point — "the top 100 cases my team can review daily". The relevant numbers are precision@k / PR-AUC and recall at the real alert budget; PR curves expose what ROC hides because precision has the positives in the denominator.

Also check calibration: a great ranker with miscalibrated probabilities breaks any downstream expected-value logic. Reliability curve + Brier score; fix with Platt scaling or isotonic regression on a held-out set.
Then set the threshold from the cost matrix, not at 0.5 — expected-cost minimization or the budget constraint, revisited whenever costs or prevalence drift.
Meta-answer: metric-model mismatch is a framing failure — agree on the operating metric with the business before training, not after.
drill.oneLiner: ROC-AUC averages over all thresholds and ignores prevalence — the business operates at one budgeted threshold, so I'd evaluate precision and recall at that budget, check calibration, and set the threshold from the cost matrix.
drill.followUp: "When would you still prefer ROC-AUC?" → comparing rankers across datasets with different prevalence, or when the operating point isn't fixed yet.

questions.text: Your XGBoost probabilities feed an expected-value calculation. What's wrong with using them raw?
points: Boosted trees are not calibrated — outputs are pushed toward 0 and 1, they rank well but misprice
Expected value multiplies probability by money, so miscalibration becomes a wrong bid
Fix: Platt scaling (sigmoid) or isotonic on a held-out calibration set — never on training folds
Isotonic needs more data and can overfit small sets; Platt is the safer default
Diagnose with a reliability curve plus Brier score, not accuracy
questions.badge: Trending — calibration questions recur on LeetCode Discuss + quant/risk JDs (2025–26)
questions.flow: reliability curve → calibrate on held-out data → re-check Brier → then compute EV
questions.trap: assuming a good AUC implies usable probabilities

drill.prompt: from jbtiq_ml Q25: "Your XGBoost model's probabilities feed an expected-value bid calculation. What's wrong with using them raw, and what do you do?"
drill.badge: Trending — calibration questions recur on LeetCode Discuss + quant/risk JDs (2025–26)
drill.hint: A model can rank perfectly and still lie about the probability. Which training objectives cause that, and what's the repair?
points: Ranking ≠ calibration: boosted trees (and anything trained with early stopping on AUC, class weights, or resampling) systematically output distorted probabilities — resampling shifts the base rate, boosting tends to push scores toward the extremes. Expected-value math multiplies by these numbers, so distortion becomes money lost.
Diagnose with a reliability diagram (predicted probability vs observed frequency, binned) and Brier score — AUC can't see the problem at all.

Repair: fit a post-hoc calibrator on a held-out set (never the training data): Platt scaling (sigmoid — low data, monotone distortion) or isotonic regression (more flexible, needs more data, can overfit small sets). If you resampled, also correct for the shifted prior.
Operational detail: calibration drifts with the population — recalibrate on recent data as part of retraining cadence, and monitor observed-vs-predicted rates in production as the canary.
Say the general rule: any time the probability itself (not the rank) enters a decision — pricing, EV, risk thresholds — calibration is a requirement, not a nicety.
drill.oneLiner: Boosted trees rank well but lie about probabilities, and EV math consumes the lie — so I check a reliability diagram, fit Platt or isotonic on held-out data, and monitor observed-versus-predicted rates for drift.

questions.text: The positive class is 0.3%. How do you sample, split and measure?
points: Stratify every split; at that rate a random fold can hold almost no positives
Prefer class weights / cost-sensitive learning over resampling — no synthetic data, no distribution lie
Resample inside the CV fold only; SMOTE before splitting is leakage with extra steps
SMOTE interpolates — meaningless for categoricals and often for high-dimensional data
Report PR-AUC, precision@k, recall at a fixed alert budget — never accuracy

drill.prompt: from jbtiq_ml Q9: "Your positive class is 0.3% of the data. How do you sample and split so that your metrics mean anything?"
drill.badge: Trending — recurs on LeetCode Discuss (fraud/anomaly framing) + JDs (2025–26)
drill.hint: Two different mistakes: resampling in the wrong place, and evaluating on a resampled set. Which one silently invalidates the number?
points: Stratify every split on the target so each fold has enough positives; with 0.3% and small folds, positives-per-fold becomes the binding constraint — use repeated stratified K-fold to reduce variance in the estimate.

Never resample the validation or test set. Resampling (SMOTE/undersampling) belongs inside the training fold only, applied after the split. Evaluating on a balanced set gives a number that doesn't exist in production. This is the single most common error here.

Metric choice: accuracy is meaningless (99.7% by predicting negative). Use PR-AUC / average precision rather than ROC-AUC — with extreme imbalance ROC-AUC is dominated by the huge negative class and looks flattering. Report precision@k or recall at a fixed alert budget, because that's how the system is actually used.

Prefer class weights / scale_pos_weight and threshold tuning over synthetic oversampling as the first move — cheaper, no synthetic-neighbour artifacts, and preserves calibration better. SMOTE on high-dimensional or categorical data interpolates nonsense.

Report confidence intervals — with ~300 positives per 100k rows, differences of a point or two are noise. And say it: with imbalance, the real deliverable is a ranked list under a review-capacity budget, not a classifier.
drill.oneLiner: Stratify the splits, resample only inside the training fold, evaluate with PR-AUC and precision at the real alert budget — and reach for class weights and threshold tuning before SMOTE.

questions.text: Random Forest or XGBoost for a new tabular problem — how do you actually choose?
points: RF: parallel, low-variance, forgiving — near-zero tuning, a strong honest baseline in an hour
XGBoost/LightGBM: sequential, bias-reducing — higher ceiling, more tuning, more overfit risk
Boosting is the more sensitive to noisy labels and to leakage — it will happily exploit both
LightGBM for wide/large data (leaf-wise, histogram), CatBoost for heavy categoricals
Real answer: RF as the baseline you must beat, boosting as the model you ship
questions.badge: Trending — recurs on LeetCode Discuss + virtually every tabular-ML JD (2025–26)
questions.flow: RF baseline first → boost for the ceiling → tune only if the gap justifies it
questions.trap: starting with XGBoost tuning before you have a baseline to beat

drill.prompt: from jbtiq_ml Q28: "Random Forest or XGBoost for a new tabular problem — how do you actually choose?"
drill.badge: Trending — recurs on LeetCode Discuss + virtually every tabular-ML JD (2025–26)
drill.hint: Don't answer with "XGBoost is better". Answer with the conditions under which each one earns its keep.
points: RF when: you want strong results with almost no tuning, robustness to noisy labels and outliers, easy parallel training, honest internal validation via OOB score, and you value stability over the last few points of accuracy. RF rarely embarrasses you.

GBM (XGBoost/LightGBM/CatBoost) when: you can pay the tuning cost (learning rate, depth, subsampling, early stopping on a validation set) for typically better accuracy, you need native missing-value handling, custom objectives (quantile, ranking), or built-in regularization. LightGBM for scale/speed (leaf-wise growth), CatBoost when categorical features dominate (ordered boosting fights target leakage).
Failure asymmetry: RF's danger is mediocrity; GBM's danger is overfitting noisy labels and drifting data — boosting chases residuals, and residuals of noise are noise.
Modern caveat worth saying: on tabular data these still routinely beat deep learning; the deep-tabular literature keeps re-finding that. Don't reach for a neural net to signal sophistication.
Practical answer: train both with defaults + logistic regression as the floor; the gaps tell you where the signal is and whether tuning is worth it.
drill.oneLiner: RF is the robust low-tuning default with OOB validation; boosting buys more accuracy, custom objectives and missing-value handling at the price of a tuning and overfitting budget — I train both against a logistic floor and let the gaps decide.

questions.text: Why does bagging reduce variance while boosting reduces bias? Mechanism, not slogans.
points: Bagging: independent-ish models on bootstrap samples → averaging cancels uncorrelated error
Decorrelation is the point — RF adds feature subsampling because bootstrap alone leaves trees too alike
Boosting: each learner fits the residual/gradient of the ensemble so far → systematically reduces bias
Which is why bagging wants deep (low-bias, high-variance) trees and boosting wants shallow stumps
Boosting has no variance-cancelling mechanism — hence learning rate, early stopping, subsampling
questions.flow: bagging averages independent errors → boosting fits what's left over → depth follows from that
questions.trap: "bagging is parallel, boosting is sequential" — that's the implementation, not the mechanism

drill.prompt: from jbtiq_ml Q27: "Why does bagging reduce variance while boosting reduces bias? Mechanism, not slogans."
drill.badge: Evergreen
drill.hint: What does averaging do to independent errors? And what does each boosting round fit on?
points: Bagging: train high-variance learners (deep trees) on bootstrap samples and average — averaging n imperfectly-correlated estimators shrinks variance roughly with n, discounted by their correlation. Bias is untouched: the average of biased models is still biased.

Random Forest's extra trick is decorrelation: random feature subsets per split make trees disagree more, and the variance reduction depends on that decorrelation — that's why max_features matters more than n_estimators.

Boosting: sequential — each learner fits the residuals/gradients of the current ensemble, so the ensemble incrementally corrects systematic error → bias falls. Weak learners (shallow trees) keep per-round variance low; overfitting arrives through too many rounds, hence early stopping and the learning rate.
Formal frame: gradient boosting is gradient descent in function space — each tree is a step along the negative gradient of the loss. Saying that sentence is the senior tell.
Consequences: bagging parallelizes trivially and is robust to tuning; boosting is sequential, more tunable, usually more accurate, and more able to overfit noisy labels.
drill.oneLiner: Bagging averages decorrelated high-variance learners so variance falls; boosting fits each new learner to the ensemble's residuals — gradient descent in function space — so bias falls.

questions.text: SHAP vs LIME in one minute — and what neither of them can tell you.
points: SHAP: Shapley values from game theory — additive, consistent, also gives a global view
LIME: local surrogate on perturbed samples — cheap, model-agnostic, unstable run to run
SHAP costs compute; TreeSHAP makes it tractable, which is why it dominates tabular
Neither gives causality — they explain the model's function, not the world
Both mislead under correlated features — perturbation samples go off-manifold

drill.prompt: from jbtiq_ml Q37: "SHAP vs LIME in one minute — and what neither of them can tell you."
drill.badge: Evergreen
drill.hint: One has axiomatic guarantees, one fits a local surrogate. The trap in the question is the last clause.
points: SHAP: allocates a prediction's deviation from the baseline across features using Shapley values — consistency and local-accuracy guarantees (attributions sum to the prediction), exact + fast for trees via TreeSHAP, expensive for arbitrary models. Global views come from aggregating local values.

LIME: fits an interpretable local surrogate (sparse linear model) around one prediction by perturbing inputs — model-agnostic and intuitive, but unstable (perturbation kernel and sampling change the story) with no consistency guarantees. Two runs can disagree; that alone makes SHAP the default where it's tractable.
Both inherit the correlation problem: perturbing features independently creates unrealistic data points, and credit spreads across correlated features arbitrarily.

What neither tells you: causality or fairness. They explain the model's function, so a leaky or proxy-discriminatory feature shows up as "important" without any flag that it's wrong to use. Explanation ≠ justification — that's the clause the interviewer wants.
Production use: SHAP for reason codes and debugging (leakage hunting via absurdly-important features), with humans reviewing whether the model's reasons are acceptable reasons.
drill.oneLiner: SHAP gives axiomatically consistent attributions and LIME gives an unstable local surrogate — but both explain the model, not reality, so neither can tell you whether an important feature is leakage or a discriminatory proxy.

questions.text: How do you guarantee training and serving compute a feature identically?
points: One definition, one code path — two implementations always diverge, usually silently
Feature store with the same transformation used offline and online is the structural answer
Point-in-time correctness: join features as they were at the event, not as they are now
Ship the preprocessing inside the model artefact (pipeline object), not in the calling service
Detect it anyway: log serving features, replay them offline, compare distributions
questions.badge: Trending — recurs on ML system design loops + feature-store JDs (2025–26)
questions.flow: one definition → point-in-time joins → preprocessing inside the artefact → log and replay
questions.trap: a "small" reimplementation of the feature in the serving service

drill.prompt: from jbtiq_ml Q43: "Design the serving architecture for a churn model: where do features come from, and how do you guarantee training and serving compute them identically?"
drill.badge: Trending — recurs on ML system design loops + feature-store JDs (2025–26)
drill.hint: The failure you're designing against has a name. What are the two "as-of" guarantees a feature platform gives you?
points: The enemy is train-serve skew: training features computed in SQL over the warehouse, serving features computed in application code — two implementations drift, and the model quietly degrades. The design goal is one feature definition, two materializations.

A feature store (Feast/Tecton pattern) provides exactly that: an offline store for training with point-in-time-correct joins (features as-of each historical label's timestamp — no future leakage), and an online store (low-latency KV) serving the same definitions at request time, with a materialization pipeline keeping them in sync.

Serving shape by latency need: batch-score nightly into a table if decisions are daily (churn usually is — say this; it removes most of the infra); online endpoint + online store only if the decision is truly per-request; streaming aggregations only for features that must be fresh in seconds.
Wrap the model behind a prediction service contract (schema-validated inputs, versioned model + features together) so feature and model versions roll forward and back atomically.

Monitoring is part of the architecture, not an afterthought: feature null-rates and distributions vs training profile, prediction distribution drift, and delayed-label metrics joining outcomes back for true performance.
drill.oneLiner: One feature definition materialized twice — an offline store with point-in-time joins for training and an online store serving the identical values — versioned atomically with the model; and for churn I'd argue for nightly batch scoring before building any of the online path.
drill.followUp: "You don't have a feature store and can't buy one." → share one computation library/dbt layer between paths, log served features and reuse them as training data (log-and-wait).

questions.text: 📝 "Live metrics degraded 6 points over two months. Build me the decision framework.
points: Separate three: data drift (inputs move) · concept drift (X→y moves) · label delay
Data drift is detectable without labels — PSI, KS, per-feature stability
Concept drift needs labels — a degraded metric may just be labels arriving
Rule out non-drift causes: upstream schema change, broken join, new client version
Retrain trigger = threshold on the business metric, not a calendar; compare against incumbent
questions.badge: Trending — drift + retraining cadence recurs across MLOps JDs + LeetCode Discuss (2025–26)
questions.flow: is it drift or a pipeline bug? → data vs concept → label lag → threshold-triggered retrain
questions.trap: a nightly retrain cron as the answer to drift

drill.prompt: from jbtiq_ml Q44: "The model's live metrics degraded 6 points over two months. Build me the decision framework: drift types, how you detect each, and when you retrain."
drill.badge: Trending — drift + retraining cadence recurs across MLOps JDs + LeetCode Discuss (2025–26)
drill.hint: Three different things can drift, and only one of them is visible without labels. Retraining fixes some of them and not others.
points: Taxonomy: covariate shift (P(X) moved — new user mix), label shift (P(y) moved — churn rate changed), concept drift (P(y|X) moved — the relationship changed, e.g. post-pricing-change behaviour). Retraining on recent data fixes the first two; concept drift may also need new features or a rethink.

Detection layers: without labels — per-feature distribution monitors (PSI/KS) and prediction-distribution drift; with (delayed) labels — rolling live metrics joined against outcomes, sliced per segment because aggregate metrics hide localized rot.

Diagnose before retraining: rule out the impostors — data pipeline breakage (nulls, unit changes, schema drift) and upstream product changes produce identical symptoms and retraining just bakes them in.

Retraining policy options: scheduled (simple, predictable), trigger-based on drift/metric thresholds (responsive, needs good monitors), or continual (rarely worth the validation risk). Every retrain goes through the same offline gate + shadow/canary as a new model — automation without evaluation is how you ship a regression at 3am.
Architect the meta-question: measure time-to-detect and time-to-recover as SLOs for the ML system; the drift response is an operational loop, not an event.
drill.oneLiner: Split it into covariate, label and concept drift — monitor feature and prediction distributions labels-free plus delayed-label metrics per segment, rule out pipeline breakage first, and retrain through the same canary gate on either a schedule or a drift trigger.

questions.text: You target-encoded a 5,000-level categorical and validation AUC jumped. Why be suspicious?
points: Target encoding puts the label into a feature — the jump is usually leakage, not signal
Worst on high-cardinality: rare levels encode to essentially their own target value
Safe version: out-of-fold encoding, smoothing toward the global mean, noise injection
Fit the encoder inside the CV fold, never on the full training set
Alternatives that don't leak: frequency encoding, hashing, or let CatBoost do ordered target statistics

questions.badge: Trending — recurs on LeetCode Discuss + Kaggle-adjacent interview posts (2025–26)
questions.flow: suspect leakage → out-of-fold encoding + smoothing → refit inside the fold → re-measure
questions.trap: celebrating the AUC jump and shipping it

drill.prompt: from jbtiq_ml Q11: "You target-encoded a 5,000-level categorical and validation AUC jumped. Why should you be suspicious, and how do you do it safely?"
drill.badge: Trending — recurs on LeetCode Discuss + Kaggle-adjacent interview posts (2025–26)
drill.hint: The encoding contains the target. What has to be true about which rows contributed to each row's encoding?
points: Target encoding replaces a level with a statistic of the target itself, so any row whose own label leaks into its encoding gets a feature that partially is the answer — the AUC jump is often self-leakage, not signal.
Safe construction: out-of-fold encoding (each row encoded using folds it isn't in) or leave-one-out, computed strictly inside the training data of each CV fold — never on the full dataset.
Rare levels need smoothing (shrink toward the global mean weighted by level count) or they memorise individual rows; unseen levels at serving time need an explicit fallback to the prior.

Compare against the honest alternatives for high cardinality: frequency/count encoding (no target, no leakage), feature hashing (bounded width, collisions as a controlled cost), or entity embeddings if you're already in a neural setting.
Verify with a time-split holdout, not random CV — target encoding failures are exactly the kind random CV hides.
drill.oneLiner: A jump after target encoding is guilty until proven innocent — encode out-of-fold with smoothing inside each training fold, define the unseen-level fallback, and confirm on a time-split.

Position bias: offline relevance ignores that rank 1 wins clicks regardless
Shift at serve time: cold users, new items, candidates the offline set never held
Plus the boring one: a skew bug — different features online than in replay
Interleaving or A/B settles it; offline metrics are a filter, never a verdict

questions.flow: name the bias (presentation → position → shift) → check for skew → settle with A/B
questions.trap: trusting an offline ranking metric as a launch decision

drill.prompt: from jbtiq_ml Q42: "Your recommender's offline NDCG improved but online CTR dropped after deploy. Give me three mechanisms that produce exactly this."
drill.badge: Trending — offline-online divergence recurs on LeetCode Discuss + rec-sys JDs (2025–26)
drill.hint: Think about what the offline dataset can't contain: what generated it, what's missing from it, and what the metric ignores.
points: Feedback-loop bias: your offline data was logged under the old policy — items the old model never showed have no labels, so offline eval rewards agreeing with the old model more than being right (off-policy evaluation problem). A genuinely different-and-better ranker can score worse offline.
Position/presentation bias: NDCG on logged clicks inherits position bias — users click what was ranked high; the new model reshuffles positions and inherits none of that logged advantage.

Diversity/novelty collapse: NDCG is per-list relevance — a model that maximizes it can converge on near-duplicate popular items, and users respond to staleness by clicking less; the aggregate experience degrades in a way per-query metrics can't see.
Also check the boring ones: train-serve skew in features, latency regression suppressing impressions, and the metric population (NDCG on all users vs CTR concentrated in heavy users).
The architectural lesson: offline metrics gate deployment, online A/B decides it; and log propensities (exposure probabilities) so future offline eval can be counterfactually corrected (IPS-style).
drill.oneLiner: Logged data was generated by the old policy, so offline NDCG rewards imitating it — add position bias and diversity collapse, and offline-up-online-down is expected; the fix is propensity logging, counterfactual eval, and letting the A/B decide.

questions.text: What is backpropagation, really — 60 seconds, no buzzwords.
points: Chain rule applied in reverse over the computation graph — that's the whole idea
Forward pass caches activations; backward pass reuses them (memoisation, not re-derivation)
Each node receives an upstream gradient, multiplies by its local Jacobian, passes it down
Cost is roughly one forward pass — that's why it scales; the memory is the activations
Gradient checkpointing trades that memory back for recompute
questions.badge: Evergreen — the opener; the filter is whether you say "chain rule" and "reuse" in the same breath.
questions.flow: forward caches → reverse chain rule → local Jacobian × upstream gradient → parameter grads
questions.trap: describing it as "the error propagates back" without naming the chain rule

drill.prompt: from jbtiq_dl Q1: "You have 60 seconds: what is backpropagation, really — no buzzwords."
drill.badge: Evergreen — the opener; the filter is whether you say "chain rule" and "reuse" in the same breath.
drill.hint: It's two ideas glued together — one from calculus, one from algorithm design. Name both.
points: The chain rule applied over a computational graph: every op knows its local derivative; compose them backwards from the loss.

It's reverse-mode autodiff: one backward sweep yields ∂L/∂θ for every parameter, at a cost of roughly two forward passes — regardless of parameter count. Forward-mode would cost one pass per parameter.
The efficiency is memoization: cache forward activations, reuse each upstream gradient once. That cache is why activations, not weights, dominate training memory.
Backprop is not a learning rule — it only computes gradients. The optimizer (SGD/Adam) is a separate, swappable component.
drill.oneLiner: Backprop is the chain rule organized as dynamic programming over the computation graph — one backward sweep gives every parameter's gradient for about the price of two forward passes.
drill.followUp: "Why do activations dominate training memory?" → they're cached for the backward pass; recomputing them is exactly what activation checkpointing trades.

questions.text: A 12-layer sigmoid MLP trains at the top but the first layers barely move. Mechanism and three fixes.
points: Vanishing gradients: sigmoid derivative peaks at 0.25 — multiply twelve of those and it's ~10⁻⁷
Early layers therefore get a gradient orders of magnitude smaller than the last ones
Fix 1: ReLU-family activations — derivative 1 in the positive region, no shrink
Fix 2: residual connections — a gradient highway that skips the multiplicative chain
Fix 3: normalisation (BatchNorm/LayerNorm) + He initialisation to hold variance across depth
questions.flow: saturating derivative → product shrinks with depth → ReLU + residuals + norm/init
questions.trap: blaming the learning rate

drill.prompt: from jbtiq_dl Q4: "A 12-layer sigmoid MLP trains fine at the top, but the first layers' weights barely move. Explain the mechanism and give me three fixes."
drill.badge: Evergreen
drill.hint: The gradient at layer 1 is a product of how many terms? What is the maximum value of a sigmoid's derivative?
points: Vanishing gradient: backprop multiplies one Jacobian per layer; sigmoid's derivative is at most 0.25, so twelve of them shrink the signal roughly exponentially with depth.
The same multiplication can explode if weight scales sit above 1 — vanish/explode are two ends of one mechanism (spectral radius of the layer Jacobians).
Fixes, in the order you'd try them: ReLU-family activations, variance-preserving init (He/Xavier), normalization layers, residual connections for real depth.
Diagnosis you'd actually run: log per-layer gradient norms — a clean exponential decay across layers is the signature.
drill.oneLiner: Gradients at the bottom are a product of a dozen Jacobians, each shrunk by sigmoid's ≤0.25 derivative — so I swap activations, fix init, add normalization, and use residuals if depth is non-negotiable.
drill.followUp: "Which of those fixes made truly deep networks possible?" → residual connections — they give gradients an identity path around every layer.

questions.text: Why cross-entropy and not MSE for classification?
points: With sigmoid/softmax, MSE's gradient carries the activation derivative — it vanishes exactly when the model is confidently wrong
Cross-entropy's gradient through softmax is simply (prediction − target) — large error, large step
CE is the negative log-likelihood of the model's distribution; it's the principled loss, not a trick
MSE also treats class probabilities as distances, which they aren't
Corollary worth saying: CE punishes confident wrongness harshly — that's the feature
questions.flow: MSE + sigmoid → vanishing gradient when wrong → CE gives (pred − target) → NLL is the reason
questions.trap: "cross-entropy just works better" with no mechanism

drill.prompt: from jbtiq_dl Q5: "Why cross-entropy and not MSE for classification? Most candidates say 'it just works better' — you have to do better than that."
drill.badge: Evergreen
drill.hint: Differentiate the loss through the sigmoid in both cases. What term is present in the MSE gradient that cross-entropy cancels?
points: Cross-entropy is maximum likelihood under a categorical/Bernoulli model — it's the principled loss for probability outputs, equivalent to minimizing KL to the label distribution.

The mechanism: through sigmoid/softmax, the MSE gradient carries a σ′ factor — near-zero exactly when the model is confidently wrong, so learning stalls. Cross-entropy cancels σ′, leaving a clean (p − y) gradient.
MSE on probabilities also makes the optimization landscape non-convex in the logits with flat plateaus; CE stays well-behaved.
Practical corollary: pair softmax with CE via the fused, numerically stable op — never hand-compose log(softmax) (ties back to Q2).
drill.oneLiner: Cross-entropy is MLE for classification and its gradient is just (p − y) — MSE keeps a σ′ factor that goes to zero precisely when the model is confidently wrong.

questions.text: A teammate initialises all weights to zero 'for reproducibility'. What happens?
points: Symmetry never breaks — every unit in a layer gets identical gradients and stays identical forever
The layer collapses to the capacity of one neuron, whatever its width
Init's real job: keep activation and gradient variance stable across depth
Xavier/Glorot for symmetric activations (tanh, sigmoid), He for ReLU — the factor-of-2 is the dead half
Reproducibility comes from seeding, not from a constant

questions.flow: identical gradients → symmetry holds → layer = one neuron; init for variance, seed for repro
questions.trap: confusing determinism with initialisation

drill.prompt: from jbtiq_dl Q24: "A teammate initializes all weights to zero 'for reproducibility'. What happens, and what should initialization actually be doing?"
drill.badge: Evergreen
drill.hint: If two neurons in a layer start identical, what keeps them identical? Then: what statistical property should a good init preserve layer to layer?
points: Zero (or any constant) init → symmetry: every neuron in a layer computes the same output and receives the same gradient, forever — the layer collapses to one effective neuron. With ReLU, zero init is also simply dead.
Init's real job: preserve activation and gradient variance across layers, so signals neither vanish nor explode before training starts.
Xavier/Glorot (scales by fan-in/fan-out) suits tanh/sigmoid; He (2/fan_in) corrects for ReLU zeroing half its inputs.
Transformer practice: additionally down-scale residual-branch output projections (by depth) so the network starts close to the identity — init and the residual stream cooperate.
Random init breaks symmetry; the scale is what the named schemes are actually about.
drill.oneLiner: Constant init makes every neuron in a layer the same neuron forever — real init breaks symmetry and sets scales (Xavier for saturating activations, He for ReLU) so variance survives the depth.

questions.text: Dropout was left in train mode during evaluation. Explain exactly what that does.
points: Train mode: randomly zeroes units each forward pass, scaling the survivors (inverted dropout)
Eval mode: no zeroing, full network, deterministic
Left on at eval → predictions differ run to run on the same input, and average quality drops
The signature symptom: non-reproducible eval numbers with no data or seed change
Same class of bug as BatchNorm using batch statistics at inference instead of running estimates
questions.flow: train zeroes + rescales → eval must be deterministic → symptom is a shifting eval number
questions.trap: chasing a data bug when the symptom is run-to-run variance

drill.prompt: from jbtiq_dl Q27: "A junior reports the model gives noticeably different predictions between two 'identical' evaluation runs. You find dropout was left in train mode. Explain exactly what it does in each mode and why this bug looks like that."
drill.badge: Evergreen
drill.hint: What does inverted dropout do to the surviving activations at train time — and what should eval mode be instead?
points: Train mode: each unit is zeroed with probability p → prevents co-adaptation; the net effect is training a shifting ensemble of subnetworks.
Inverted dropout scales survivors by 1/(1−p) at train time, so expected activations match — which is what allows eval mode to be a clean identity (no scaling, no randomness).

Left in train mode at eval: predictions become stochastic run-to-run — exactly the reported symptom. Same bug class: BatchNorm using batch statistics instead of running stats. model.eval() flips both.

Transformer placement: attention weights, residual outputs, embeddings. Modern nuance worth saying: large single-epoch LLM pretraining typically sets dropout to zero — in the underfitting regime, data scale is the regularizer.
drill.oneLiner: Train-mode dropout randomly zeroes units and rescales survivors so eval can be the identity — leave it on at eval and you're sampling a different subnetwork per run, which is exactly the nondeterminism reported.

questions.text: Two sick models: one has train 0.1 / val 2.3, the other is stuck at 2.3 on both. Triage each.
points: Gap = variance → regularise, augment, more data, early stopping, smaller model
No gap, both high = underfit or broken pipeline — capacity, LR, or the data is wrong
Underfit triage: can it overfit a single batch? If not, the bug is in the code
Then LR (too low = stuck, too high = noisy plateau), labels, normalisation, loss wiring
Never tune hyperparameters before the overfit-one-batch test passes
questions.flow: gap? → variance path; no gap? → overfit one batch first → then LR, labels, wiring
questions.trap: treating "loss is high" as one diagnosis

drill.prompt: from jbtiq_dl Q43: "Two sick models: one has train loss 0.1 with val loss 2.3; the other is stuck at 2.3 on both. Give me the triage for each."
drill.badge: Evergreen
drill.hint: Gap versus no-gap are different diseases. And there's one five-minute experiment that should open any DL debugging session.
points: Gap (0.1 vs 2.3) = overfitting/memorization: more or better data and augmentation first, then regularization (weight decay, dropout, early stopping on val), smaller model last. Also rule out val-set problems: leakage, distribution mismatch, mislabeled val.

No gap (2.3 / 2.3) = underfitting or a broken pipeline: sweep LR first (the most common cause in both directions), check the data/labels are actually learnable, add capacity or training time only after.
The universal opener: overfit a single tiny batch to ~zero loss. Fails → bug in loss/labels/architecture, not a tuning issue. Passes → it's data or optimization scale.
Know the numbers: for a vocab of ~50k, uniform-random cross-entropy is ~ln(50k)≈10.8 — where the loss plateaus relative to trivial baselines tells you if it learned anything at all.
LLM-era nuance: single-epoch pretraining rarely overfits classically — the gap disease there is data contamination/duplication, and the cure is data quality, not dropout.
drill.oneLiner: A train–val gap is a data-and-regularization problem, a joint plateau is an optimization-or-bug problem — and the first move in both is the tiny-batch overfit test, because it splits 'broken' from 'undertuned' in five minutes.

questions.text: Why does an RNN forget the start of a long document? Training-time mechanics, not the slogan.
points: BPTT unrolls the sequence — gradients multiply the same recurrent Jacobian per step
Spectral radius < 1 → vanishing; > 1 → exploding. Same multiplicative cause
Exploding is easy (clip); vanishing is the hard one — signal gone, not noisy
LSTM/GRU add an additive gated cell path — gradient flows without repeated multiplication
Still a longer leash, not unlimited — and inherently sequential, which transformers killed
questions.flow: BPTT multiplies Jacobians → vanish or explode → gates give an additive path → still sequential
questions.trap: saying "it has a short memory" without the multiplicative argument

drill.prompt: from jbtiq_dl Q8: "Why does an RNN forget the beginning of a long document? Walk me through the training-time mechanics, not just the slogan."
drill.badge: Evergreen
drill.hint: Unroll the network in time. What gets multiplied T times, and why is it worse than the deep-MLP case?
points: BPTT unrolls the recurrence into a T-layer graph; the gradient from step T to step 1 is a product of T Jacobians of the same recurrent weight matrix — repeated multiplication by one matrix vanishes or explodes even faster than depth with varied weights.
Vanish → early tokens contribute ~zero gradient → the model cannot learn long-range dependencies, regardless of capacity.
Explode → loss spikes; the standard patch is gradient clipping. Truncated BPTT caps the horizon, which is an admission of the problem, not a fix.
Second, independent failure: the recurrence is inherently sequential — step t needs step t−1, so training can't parallelize across the sequence. That's the throughput half of why RNNs lost.
drill.oneLiner: BPTT multiplies the same recurrent Jacobian T times, so gradients vanish or explode with sequence length — and even when it works, the serial dependency means you can't parallelize training.

questions.text: 🗣️ (jbtiq_ml Q4 · S1 Foundations & Generalization) "Parametric vs non-parametric, and instance-based vs model-based — why do these distinctions matter operationally?
points: Parametric: fixed-size parameter vector regardless of n (linear/logistic regression, naive Bayes, neural nets). Strong assumptions, cheap and constant-time inference, higher bias, needs less data.

Non-parametric: model complexity grows with the data (kNN, decision trees, kernel SVM, Gaussian processes). Fewer assumptions, higher variance, needs more data — and inference cost/memory grows with n.

Instance-based (kNN, kernel methods) stores the training data and defers all computation to query time — "lazy". Model-based compresses training data into parameters — "eager". kNN is the pathological serving case: zero training cost, expensive and memory-heavy inference, which is exactly why production kNN becomes an ANN index (FAISS/HNSW).

Operational consequences to say out loud: model artifact size, p99 inference latency, whether you can serve on CPU, whether retraining is incremental, and whether the model can be shipped to an edge device.
Non-parametric ≠ "no parameters" — it means the number isn't fixed in advance. Correcting that misconception scores points.

questions.text: 🗣️ (jbtiq_ml Q5 · S1 Foundations & Generalization) "Your training set doesn't fit in memory and new data arrives continuously. Batch, online, or out-of-core — how do you decide, and what breaks in each?
points: Separate the constraints: size → out-of-core / mini-batch training (partial_fit, chunked readers, distributed training). Recency/drift → online or frequently-retrained batch. Streaming data does not automatically require online learning.

Batch retraining on a schedule is the boring, correct default: reproducible, easy to validate and roll back, and you can A/B the new model. Most "we need online learning" requirements are satisfied by retraining daily plus fresh features at serving time.

True online learning breaks in specific ways: no clean train/test separation, catastrophic drift from a bad data burst, poisoning risk, no reproducibility, and hyperparameters (learning rate) that must be robust forever. You also lose the ability to validate before shipping.

Out-of-core caveats: shuffling is hard (so mini-batches may be correlated), feature scaling needs running statistics, and only some algorithms support incremental fitting (SGD-based linear models, naive Bayes, some trees — not vanilla RF/SVM).

Architect answer: decouple freshness of features from freshness of weights. A daily-retrained model with real-time features usually beats an online-updated model with stale features, and it's far easier to operate.

questions.text: 🗣️ (jbtiq_ml Q8 · S2 Data, EDA, Splits & Leakage) "You've got a new 40-million-row, 300-column dataset and one day. What's your EDA plan, and what are you actually looking for?
points: Frame EDA as producing decisions, not charts: what's the target's base rate, which columns are unusable, what's the split strategy, which features need what transform, and is there leakage.

Order of operations: sample first (stratified, so it fits in memory) → schema/dtype audit → missingness pattern (per column and jointly — is missingness informative?) → target distribution and base rate → cardinality of categoricals → duplicates and near-duplicates → per-feature target relationship (bivariate) → correlation/collinearity clusters → temporal coverage and per-period stability.

Actively hunt: too-good features (near-perfect correlation with the target = leakage), IDs disguised as numbers, constant/near-constant columns, categorical levels that only appear after a date (schema change), unit inconsistencies, sentinel values (−999, 1900-01-01) masquerading as data.
Automated tools (ydata-profiling, sweetviz) for the first pass to save hours — then targeted manual work on the suspicious columns. Say that you don't trust an automated report as the analysis.

Deliverable at end of day: a data quality note (issues + decisions), the split strategy, a feature shortlist, and a trained baseline. A baseline model is part of EDA — it tells you which columns matter.
questions.badge: Evergreen (asked in almost every ML loop as a "how do you work" probe)
questions.oneLiner: Sample, then audit schema, missingness, base rate, cardinality and duplicates — hunting specifically for leakage and sentinel values — and finish the day with a documented data-quality note, a split strategy and a baseline.

questions.text: 🗣️ (jbtiq_ml Q10 · S3 Feature Engineering) "When does feature scaling actually matter, and when is it a no-op? Give me the rule, not the ritual.
points: Scaling matters where the algorithm compares or combines feature magnitudes: distance-based (kNN, K-means, SVM-RBF), gradient-descent-trained models (linear/logistic with SGD, neural nets — conditioning of the loss surface), and regularized linear models (the penalty is scale-sensitive, so unscaled features get unequal shrinkage).
Tree-based models are scale-invariant — splits depend on order, not magnitude. Scaling RF/XGBoost inputs is ritual, not engineering.

Choice: standardization (z-score) as default; MinMax when a bounded range is needed; RobustScaler when outliers would dominate the mean/std; log/power transforms (Box-Cox/Yeo-Johnson) for heavy skew — that's changing the shape, not just the scale.
The operational rule: fit the scaler on train only, inside the pipeline/fold — scaling on the full data is quiet leakage.
PCA is the sneaky case: it maximises variance, so unscaled features with big units dominate the components.

links.target: 01-ML/03-Feature-engineering/03-When Scaling Matters (and When It Doesn't — Tree Models)

questions.oneLiner: Scale for distance-, gradient- and penalty-based models, skip it for trees — and always fit the scaler inside the training fold, because the penalty and the components see raw magnitudes.

questions.text: 🗣️ (jbtiq_ml Q12 · S3 Feature Engineering) "Why do sklearn Pipelines and ColumnTransformer matter architecturally — beyond code tidiness?
points: Leakage guarantee: a Pipeline refits every transform inside each CV fold automatically, so imputers/scalers/encoders never see validation rows. Doing transforms "once, up front" is the classic silent leak — the Pipeline makes the correct thing the default thing.

Train-serve consistency: the fitted pipeline is one serialized artifact containing preprocessing and model, so serving applies byte-identical transforms — the cheap version of what a feature store solves at platform scale.
ColumnTransformer binds transforms to columns declaratively — numeric vs categorical vs text paths in one object, no hand-maintained index bookkeeping to drift.
Hyperparameter search extends over preprocessing choices too (imputer__strategy, encoder type) in one GridSearchCV/Optuna space — tuning the whole function, not just the estimator.
Architect framing: the pipeline is a contract — schema in, prediction out — which makes it testable, versionable, and swappable behind an API.
questions.badge: Trending — recurs on ML-Engineer JDs ("productionize sklearn pipelines") + LinkedIn (2025–26)
questions.oneLiner: A Pipeline makes leakage-free CV the default and ships preprocessing and model as one versioned artifact — it's train-serve consistency in miniature.

questions.text: 🗣️ (jbtiq_ml Q13 · S4 Missing Data & Outliers) "MCAR, MAR, MNAR — why does the mechanism of missingness change what you're allowed to do?
points: MCAR (missing completely at random): missingness independent of everything → dropping rows (CCA) is unbiased, just wasteful. The only case where deletion is safe, and the rarest in practice.

MAR (missing at random given observed data): missingness explained by other observed columns → model-based imputation (KNN, MICE/IterativeImputer) is justified because the observed columns carry the recovery signal.

MNAR (missing not at random): the missingness depends on the unobserved value itself (income blank because it's high) → no imputation is unbiased; the honest move is a missing-indicator feature plus a sentinel/category, letting the model learn from the missingness itself.
Practical test: you can't prove the mechanism from data alone — reason from the data-generating process (form logic, sensor behaviour), and check whether missingness correlates with other columns.
Production rule: whatever the choice, the imputer is fitted on train only and shipped in the pipeline, and the serving path must handle "column entirely absent", not just NaN.

links.label: Missingness Types — MCAR, MAR, MNAR
links.target: 01-ML/04-Missing Data & Outliers/01-Missingness Types — MCAR, MAR, MNAR

links.label: Multivariate Imputation — KNN Imputer & MICE

questions.oneLiner: Deletion is only safe under MCAR, model-based imputation assumes MAR, and under MNAR the missingness is signal — so I add an indicator and let the model use it rather than pretend to recover the value.

questions.text: 🗣️ (jbtiq_ml Q14 · S4 Missing Data & Outliers) "Your fraud model's key feature has 30% missing values in production but only 2% in training. What went wrong and what do you do?
points: Diagnose the discrepancy first: training data was likely backfilled from a warehouse where the value eventually arrives, but at serving time it isn't available yet — a temporal availability skew, i.e. the training feature used the future. Alternatives: an upstream pipeline broke, or a schema/logging change.
If it's availability skew, imputation is a band-aid on leakage: the honest fix is to rebuild the feature as-of prediction time (point-in-time correctness — the thing feature stores enforce).

If it's a genuine upstream regression: page the owning team, and meanwhile check whether the model degrades gracefully — trees with native missing-handling (XGBoost/LightGBM) route NaNs learned-ly; a pipeline with a fitted imputer at least doesn't crash.

Guard against the next one: data-quality monitors on feature null rates and distributions at serving time, alerting on divergence from training profiles — this failure class is invisible in model metrics until the damage is done.
Retrain consideration: if 30% missing is the new normal, retrain with that reality (indicator + imputation) so train and serve match again.

links.target: 01-ML/04-Missing Data & Outliers/02-Imputation — CCA, Mean-Median, Mode, Random Sample, End-of-Distribution

questions.oneLiner: A train-serve gap in null rates usually means the training feature was backfilled with the future — I fix point-in-time correctness rather than impute over leakage, and put null-rate monitors on every serving feature.

questions.text: 🗣️ (jbtiq_ml Q15 · S4 Missing Data & Outliers) "When do you remove an outlier, when do you cap it, and when is the outlier the whole point?
points: Classify by origin: error outliers (sensor glitch, unit mix-up, impossible values) → correct or remove; legitimate extremes (a real whale customer) → keep, maybe transform; the target phenomenon itself (fraud, anomalies) → they're the positives, touching them destroys the task.

Detection is model-relative: z-score assumes normality, IQR is robust, Isolation Forest / LOF / One-Class SVM for multivariate shape — but detection only flags, the decision needs the origin classification.

Capping/winsorization is the middle path for legitimate heavy tails feeding scale-sensitive models (linear, distance-based); trees mostly don't care, so for tree models the answer is often "do nothing".
Whatever you do must live in the pipeline with thresholds fitted on train only — hand-deleting rows before the split is unreproducible and leaky.
Senior framing: log what you removed and why; an outlier policy is a data contract decision, and silently deleting inconvenient rows is how audit findings start.

questions.oneLiner: First decide whether the outlier is an error, a legitimate extreme, or the signal itself — remove errors, cap or transform extremes for scale-sensitive models, and never touch them when anomalies are the target.

questions.text: 🗣️ (jbtiq_ml Q16 · S5 Dimensionality Reduction & Feature Selection) "The curse of dimensionality — what concretely breaks as dimensions grow, and which model families suffer first?
points: Distances concentrate: as d grows, nearest and farthest neighbours become nearly equidistant, so distance loses discriminating power → kNN, K-means, kernel methods degrade first. This also quietly degrades vector similarity search.

Density collapses: the volume you must cover grows exponentially, so any fixed dataset becomes vanishingly sparse → density estimators and local methods starve; the data needed to maintain coverage grows exponentially.

Spurious correlations multiply: with many features and finite rows, some features correlate with the target by chance → overfitting risk rises and feature selection becomes hypothesis-testing at scale.
Who resists: regularized linear models (the penalty handles d > n), trees/boosting (axis-aligned splits ignore irrelevant dimensions reasonably well), and models with built-in selection (Lasso).
Response ladder: domain-driven feature pruning → filter/wrapper/embedded selection → projection (PCA) — selection keeps interpretability, projection keeps variance.

links.label: Feature Selection — Filter methods (correlation, chi square, mutual info)
links.target: 01-ML/05-Dimentionality Reduction/02-Feature Selection — Filter methods (correlation, chi-square, mutual info)

questions.oneLiner: High dimensions make distances uninformative and data sparse, so neighbour- and density-based methods break first — regularization, trees and explicit selection are the antidotes.

questions.text: 🗣️ (jbtiq_ml Q17 · S5 Dimensionality Reduction & Feature Selection) "Explain PCA well enough that I trust you with it: what it optimizes, what it assumes, and where it silently fails.
points: Objective: find orthogonal directions of maximum variance — equivalently minimum reconstruction error. Mechanically: eigenvectors of the covariance matrix (or right singular vectors via SVD, the numerically stable route); eigenvalues = variance explained per component.

Assumptions it quietly makes: linearity (components are linear combinations), variance = relevance (high-variance directions matter), and scale comparability — unstandardized features with big units hijack the components.

Silent failures: it's unsupervised — the discriminative direction can live in a low-variance component you just discarded (class separation destroyed); non-linear manifolds (swiss roll) need Kernel PCA/UMAP; and components are uninterpretable mixtures, a real cost in regulated settings.
Choosing k: cumulative explained-variance threshold or the elbow/scree — but if the downstream task is supervised, validate k by downstream metric, not variance.
Say the supervised alternative: LDA maximizes class separation rather than variance when labels exist.

links.target: 01-ML/05-Dimentionality Reduction/06-PCA — math (covariance matrix, eigenvectors, SVD connection)

links.label: LDA (Linear Discriminant Analysis) — supervised dim reduction

questions.oneLiner: PCA finds the max-variance orthogonal directions via the covariance eigendecomposition — it assumes linear structure, comparable scales, and that variance equals relevance, and that last assumption is the one that silently kills classifiers.

questions.text: 🗣️ (jbtiq_ml Q18 · S5 Dimensionality Reduction & Feature Selection) "A colleague clusters customers on a t-SNE plot and reports the segment sizes and distances to stakeholders. What do you tell them?
points: t-SNE preserves local neighbourhoods only: inter-cluster distances are meaningless, cluster sizes/densities are artifacts (it equalizes them), and results vary with perplexity and seed — apparent clusters can appear in pure noise at the wrong perplexity.
So: it's a visualization and hypothesis-generation tool, not a clustering or measurement tool. Cluster in the original (or PCA-reduced) space, then use the embedding only to look at the result.
UMAP is faster and preserves somewhat more global structure, and supports transforming new points — but the same "don't measure the map" warning applies.

The professional fix: validate segments with cluster-quality metrics (silhouette in the clustering space), stability across seeds/samples, and — decisive for stakeholders — differences on business variables the clustering didn't see.
Tell them kindly: the plot is a map projection; you don't measure country areas on a Mercator map.
