questions.oneLiner: t-SNE preserves only local neighbourhoods — sizes and distances on the plot are artifacts — so cluster in the original space and treat the embedding as a picture, not a measurement.

questions.text: 🗣️ (jbtiq_ml Q19 · S6 Regression, Optimization & Losses) "Which linear regression assumptions actually matter in practice, and what breaks when each fails?
points: Linearity is the one that breaks predictions: if the true relationship is non-linear, the model is simply wrong — fix with transforms, polynomial/spline terms, or a different model family. Check residuals-vs-fitted for structure.

Independence of errors breaks inference and validation: autocorrelated errors (time series, grouped data) make standard errors and random CV wildly optimistic — this is the assumption people violate without noticing.

Homoscedasticity + normality of errors break intervals, not point predictions: heteroscedastic errors mean your confidence/prediction intervals lie; coefficients stay unbiased. Fix with robust standard errors, weighted LS, or modelling the variance.

No perfect multicollinearity breaks interpretation: correlated predictors give unstable, sign-flipping coefficients (huge VIF) while predictions stay fine — fatal if the deliverable is "which factor matters", harmless if it's the forecast.
Senior framing: ask what the model is for — prediction cares about linearity and independence; explanation additionally needs the inference assumptions.
questions.oneLiner: Linearity and error-independence break predictions and validation; heteroscedasticity and normality only break the intervals; multicollinearity only breaks interpretation — so which assumptions matter depends on whether the model predicts or explains.

questions.text: 🗣️ (jbtiq_ml Q20 · S6 Regression, Optimization & Losses) "Ridge vs Lasso vs Elastic Net — mechanism, geometry, and when each wins.
points: Ridge (L2) shrinks all coefficients smoothly toward zero, never to zero — the circular constraint region has no corners for the loss contours to hit. Wins with many small, correlated effects: it shares weight across correlated features and stabilizes them.

Lasso (L1) produces exact zeros — the diamond's corners sit on the axes, so the optimum lands with coordinates at zero → built-in feature selection. Wins with sparse truth (few real drivers among many candidates).

Lasso's failure mode: among correlated features it arbitrarily picks one and drops the rest (unstable selection), and it selects at most n features when p > n. Elastic Net blends both to get selection plus grouped stability.
Both assume standardized features — the penalty is scale-sensitive, so unscaled inputs get arbitrary shrinkage.
λ is chosen by CV; and say the Bayesian reading for depth: Ridge = Gaussian prior, Lasso = Laplace prior on coefficients.
questions.oneLiner: L2 shrinks smoothly and shares weight across correlated features, L1's corners give exact zeros and selection but pick arbitrarily among correlated ones — Elastic Net when I want selection that survives correlation.

questions.text: 🗣️ (jbtiq_ml Q21 · S6 Regression, Optimization & Losses) "Batch, stochastic, and mini-batch gradient descent — and why does Adam exist? Keep it mechanical.
points: Batch GD: exact gradient, one slow step per epoch, memory-bound, deterministic. SGD: one sample — cheap, noisy (the noise helps escape shallow minima, hurts convergence). Mini-batch: the production compromise — hardware-efficient vectorization plus manageable variance; batch size trades gradient noise against step throughput.
Momentum/NAG fix the direction problem: accumulate an EMA of gradients to damp oscillation across ravines and accelerate along consistent directions.

AdaGrad/RMSProp fix the per-parameter scale problem: divide by a running magnitude of past gradients so rare/sparse features get larger effective steps; RMSProp's EMA stops AdaGrad's rate from decaying to zero.

Adam = momentum + RMSProp with bias correction for the early steps — a robust default because it solves both problems at once; the caveat worth saying: adaptive methods sometimes generalize slightly worse than tuned SGD+momentum, and AdamW (decoupled weight decay) is the modern default.
Learning rate still dominates everything: schedules/warmup matter more than the choice among good optimizers.

links.label: GD Optimizers — Momentum, NAG, AdaGrad, RMSProp, Adam
links.target: 01-ML/06-Regression Models/09-GD Optimizers — Momentum, NAG, AdaGrad, RMSProp, Adam

questions.oneLiner: Mini-batch is the throughput-vs-noise compromise; momentum fixes noisy direction, RMSProp fixes per-parameter scale, and Adam is both at once with bias correction — with the learning-rate schedule still doing the heavy lifting.

questions.text: 🗣️ (jbtiq_ml Q22 · S6 Regression, Optimization & Losses) "Your regression target is order value: mostly small, occasionally huge, and the business cares about under-forecasting more than over-forecasting. Choose a loss.
points: Decompose the requirements: heavy tail → outlier-robust loss; asymmetric cost → a loss whose penalty differs by error sign. MSE fails both (squares the whales, symmetric); MAE fixes robustness only, and its constant gradient makes optimization cruder.
Huber blends MSE near zero with MAE in the tails (δ sets the crossover) — robustness with clean gradients, but still symmetric.

The direct answer: quantile (pinball) loss — training at, say, the 0.8 quantile penalizes under-prediction 4× more than over-prediction, encoding the business asymmetry in the objective rather than post-hoc fudging. Available natively in GBMs (objective="quantile").
Alternative frame: model log(order value) to tame the tail — but remember the retransformation bias, and log-MSE is still symmetric in log space.
Say the meta-point: the loss function is where business cost enters the model — choosing it by convention instead of by cost structure is the actual mistake.
questions.badge: Trending — loss-selection scenarios recur on LeetCode Discuss + ML-Engineer JDs (2025–26)
questions.oneLiner: Under-forecasting costing more is an asymmetry, so I'd train quantile loss at the quantile matching the cost ratio — Huber or a log target handles the tail, but only pinball loss encodes the asymmetry in the objective.

questions.text: 🗣️ (jbtiq_ml Q23 · S7 Classification: Models, Metrics & Thresholds) "Why is logistic regression still the first model you train in 2026? And what's it actually doing — no hand-waving about 'squashing'.
points: Mechanically: it models the log-odds as a linear function of features, trained by maximizing likelihood (minimizing cross-entropy, which is the same thing); the sigmoid is just the inverse-link from log-odds to probability. Coefficients are log-odds ratios — directly interpretable effect sizes.

Why it's first: it's the baseline that prices the problem — if boosting only beats it by a hair, the signal is linear and you ship the simple thing; any gap it can't close tells you the problem needs interactions/non-linearity.

Operational virtues: outputs are reasonably calibrated probabilities out of the box (trees aren't), millisecond scoring at any scale, tiny artifact, trivially explainable to model risk/regulators, and stable under retraining.
With regularization + good feature engineering (interactions, binning/WoE) it remains genuinely competitive on wide sparse data — ads/risk stacks kept it for decades for exactly this reason.
Multiclass: softmax generalization; the OvR-vs-multinomial distinction rarely changes outcomes but shows you know the plumbing.
questions.oneLiner: It fits a linear model on the log-odds by maximum likelihood — I train it first because it prices the problem, gives calibrated probabilities and explainable coefficients, and defines the bar any complex model must beat by enough to justify its ops cost.

questions.text: 🗣️ (jbtiq_ml Q26 · S7 Classification: Models, Metrics & Thresholds) "Decision tree, kNN, naive Bayes — each has one killer property and one disqualifying weakness. Rapid fire.
points: Decision tree — killer: human-readable rules, handles mixed types and missing values, zero preprocessing; weakness: high variance — tiny data changes restructure the tree, so a single tree is almost always dominated by its own ensemble (RF/GBM). Depth/min_samples_leaf are the bias-variance dials.

kNN — killer: zero training, arbitrarily complex boundaries, a strong lazy baseline; weakness: inference cost and the curse of dimensionality — O(n) memory and query against raw data, distances degrade as d grows, and it demands scaling. Production form is an ANN index, at which point it's a retrieval system.

Naive Bayes — killer: absurdly fast, works with tiny data and huge sparse vocabularies (text), online-updatable; weakness: the conditional-independence assumption makes its probabilities badly calibrated (over-confident) even when the ranking is decent — fine as a filter, wrong as a probability source.

The pattern to voice: each is a regime specialist — trees for interpretable tabular rules, kNN when the data is small and local structure is everything, NB for high-dimensional sparse counts — and all three are baselines that price the problem before boosting.
questions.badge: Evergreen — the comparative sweep interviewers use to test breadth quickly.
questions.oneLiner: Tree: interpretable but unstable alone; kNN: no training but pays at query time and dies in high dimensions; naive Bayes: unbeatable speed on sparse text but its independence assumption wrecks calibration.

questions.text: 🗣️ (jbtiq_ml Q29 · S8 Ensemble Methods) "Stacking added 0.4 AUC points over your best single model. Argue both sides of shipping it.
points: Mechanism check first: the meta-learner must train on out-of-fold predictions of the base models — training it on in-sample predictions is leakage and the 0.4 points may be fiction. Keep the meta-model simple (logistic/ridge); the diversity of the bases, not the cleverness of the blender, carries stacking.

For shipping: if 0.4 AUC translates to real money at your volume (ads, risk, pricing), it can dwarf the infra cost; stacking also hedges single-model failure modes when bases are genuinely diverse (linear + trees + NN).

Against: N models to version, retrain, monitor and keep consistent; multiplied inference latency and cost; drift debugging becomes "which of five models moved"; explainability degrades; and the gain often shrinks under temporal drift because the meta-weights were fit to a particular era's error structure.
Middle path to offer: capture most of the gain with cheap weighted blending of two diverse models, or distil the ensemble into a single student model for serving.
The senior line: measure the 0.4 on a time-split holdout with CIs, price it in dollars, and let the ops cost argue against it honestly.

questions.oneLiner: First verify the gain is real — out-of-fold meta-training, time-split holdout — then price it: stacking is N times the ops surface, so I ship it only when the delta is worth real money, and I try a simple blend or distillation first.

questions.text: 🗣️ (jbtiq_ml Q30 · S8 Ensemble Methods) "XGBoost's feature importances and your SHAP values rank features differently. Which do you trust and why?
points: Default (gain/split-based) importance counts training-time split usage — it's biased toward high-cardinality and continuous features (more split points), inflated by correlated features splitting credit unpredictably, and reflects the training set, not generalization.

Permutation importance measures the drop in validation performance when a feature is shuffled — closer to "what the model actually relies on", but correlated features mask each other (shuffle one, its twin covers).

SHAP allocates each prediction's deviation from baseline across features with consistency guarantees (Shapley axioms), gives local + global views, and TreeSHAP makes it exact and fast for trees — generally the most trustworthy of the three, though it too spreads credit across correlated features rather than resolving them.
None of them is causal — every one describes the model's behaviour, not the world; a leaky feature will top all three charts. Say that sentence explicitly.
Practice: use SHAP for the ranking and local explanations, permutation as a sanity cross-check, and investigate disagreements — they usually point at correlation clusters or leakage.

questions.text: 🗣️ (jbtiq_ml Q31 · S9 Unsupervised Learning) "K-Means: what is it secretly assuming about your clusters, and how do you pick K without fooling yourself?
points: The objective (within-cluster sum of squares) encodes assumptions: clusters are spherical, similar-sized, similar-density, and separable by Euclidean distance — K-Means will happily carve a crescent or a big+small pair into wrong pieces while the loss looks fine. It also always returns K clusters, structure or not.

Mechanics worth saying: Lloyd's algorithm converges only to a local optimum → K-Means++ initialization + multiple restarts; scaling is mandatory; and for scale, Mini-batch K-Means trades a little quality for a lot of throughput.

Elbow method is a heuristic read off a monotone curve — often no clean elbow exists. Silhouette (separation vs cohesion per point) is more honest; better still is stability: does the clustering survive resampling and different seeds?

Real validation is external: do the clusters differ on business variables they weren't built from, and do they stay stable month over month? A clustering nobody can action is a scatter plot with extra steps.
If shapes/densities are the problem: GMM for elliptical + soft assignment, DBSCAN/HDBSCAN for arbitrary shapes + noise points, hierarchical when you want the dendrogram, not a fixed K.

questions.oneLiner: K-Means assumes spherical equal-sized clusters and always returns exactly K of them — so I pick K with silhouette plus stability rather than the elbow, and validate on business variables the clustering never saw.

questions.text: 🗣️ (jbtiq_ml Q32 · S9 Unsupervised Learning) "DBSCAN found 40% of your points are 'noise'. Is that a bug? Walk me through what its parameters actually control.
points: Not a bug — a feature and a diagnostic. DBSCAN grows clusters from core points (≥ minPts neighbours within eps); points reachable from no core are labelled noise. 40% noise means 40% of your data doesn't sit in any region of the density you specified — either that's true (sparse, noisy data) or eps is too tight for the feature scaling you used.

eps defines the neighbourhood radius (choose via the k-distance plot knee), minPts sets the density bar (rule of thumb ≈ dimensionality + a margin). Both are meaningless without scaled features, and eps degrades in high dimensions as distances concentrate.

The structural weakness: one global eps — clusters of varying density can't all be right; the dense one merges, the sparse one shatters into noise. That's exactly what HDBSCAN fixes (density hierarchy, per-cluster extraction, only min_cluster_size to set).
Strengths that keep it in the toolbox: finds arbitrary shapes, doesn't need K, and the noise label is genuinely useful for anomaly triage.
Answer the scenario: check scaling → k-distance plot for eps → if densities visibly vary, switch to HDBSCAN rather than tuning DBSCAN harder.

questions.oneLiner: DBSCAN labels as noise whatever fails its density bar, so 40% noise is information — I'd check scaling and the k-distance plot, and if cluster densities differ that's the one-global-eps weakness, which is HDBSCAN's cue.

questions.text: 🗣️ (jbtiq_ml Q33 · S9 Unsupervised Learning) "You have no labels. How do you evaluate a clustering well enough to defend it to a skeptical stakeholder?
points: Internal metrics — silhouette, Davies-Bouldin, Calinski-Harabasz — measure cohesion vs separation, but they share the same geometric prejudices as the algorithms (favouring compact spherical clusters), so treat them as consistency checks, not truth.

Stability is stronger evidence: re-run under bootstrap resampling, seed changes, and feature perturbations; measure agreement (ARI between runs). Structure that evaporates under resampling was noise wearing a costume.

External validation is what convinces stakeholders: the clusters differ significantly on held-out variables they weren't built from (revenue, churn, support volume) and survive over time. That's the difference between "the algorithm returned groups" and "these segments exist".
The final test is actionability: name each cluster in one sentence a marketer can act on. If a cluster can't be described, it's a mathematical artifact.

Guard the meta-risk: with enough algorithms and K values you will find clusters in anything — pre-register the pipeline (features, algorithm, selection metric) before looking, or you're p-hacking geometry.

questions.text: 🗣️ (jbtiq_ml Q35 · S10 Model Selection, Validation & Tuning) "Grid search, random search, Bayesian optimization, Hyperband — when does each earn its cost?
points: Grid scales exponentially and wastes budget on dimensions that don't matter — defensible only for 1–2 params or when you need an exhaustive, auditable sweep.

Random search dominates grid because only a few hyperparameters usually matter: random sampling probes each marginal densely instead of repeating the same few values. The right default for cheap trials.

Bayesian optimization (Optuna/TPE, GP-based) builds a surrogate of score-vs-config and spends trials where improvement is probable — earns its overhead when each trial is expensive (big model, long training) and the budget is tens-not-thousands of trials. Sequential by nature, though batched variants exist.

Hyperband/successive halving attacks a different axis: cheap partial evaluations — start many configs, kill losers early at increasing budgets. Wins when learning curves are informative early (epochs, boosting rounds); combine with Bayesian sampling (BOHB / Optuna pruning) for both.

Discipline regardless of method: search on log scales for rates/regularization, fix the seed-vs-noise question (repeat top configs), keep the test set out of it, and remember tuning gains are usually smaller than one good feature.

questions.text: 🗣️ (jbtiq_ml Q36 · S10 Model Selection, Validation & Tuning) "Model A scores 0.847, model B scores 0.851 on the test set. Your PM wants to ship B. What do you say?
points: First: is 0.004 inside the noise? A single test-set number has sampling variance — bootstrap the test set for a CI on the difference, or use a paired test on per-example results (McNemar's for classification) since both models saw the same examples. With typical test sizes, 0.004 is very often a tie.
Second: selection effect — if B was chosen as the best of many candidates on this same test set, its edge is partly winner's curse (ties into the nested-CV discipline).
Third: translate to the business metric — does 0.004 AUC move revenue/cost at all after threshold re-tuning? Offline deltas this small routinely vanish online.

The professional move: if it might matter, settle it with an A/B test online measuring the business KPI; if it can't be A/B'd, demand the offline delta clear a pre-agreed practical significance bar, not just statistical.
Also weigh asymmetries the metric hides: latency, cost, calibration, robustness across segments — B can "win" on average and lose on the segment that matters.

questions.text: 🗣️ (jbtiq_ml Q38 · S11 Interpretability & Responsible ML) "Your lending model can't satisfy demographic parity and equalized odds at once. Why not, and what do you do as the architect?
points: The impossibility is structural: when base rates differ between groups, demographic parity (equal approval rates), equalized odds (equal TPR/FPR), and predictive parity (equal precision/calibration) cannot all hold simultaneously — any calibrated model with unequal base rates violates the others. This is a mathematical constraint, not a modelling bug.

So the job is not "satisfy all metrics" but choose which fairness definition matches the harm in this domain: parity of opportunity among qualified applicants (equal TPR) means something different from equal approval rates, and the choice encodes values and law, not statistics.

That choice is a governance decision: legal/compliance and product own it, documented (model cards), with the architect providing the quantified trade-off curve — what each definition costs in the others and in accuracy.

Technical levers once chosen: pre-processing (reweighing), in-processing (constrained optimization), post-processing (group-specific thresholds — simple and auditable). Removing the protected attribute alone fails — proxies carry it right back in.
Operationally: fairness metrics are monitored in production per segment, not audited once — drift breaks fairness the same way it breaks accuracy.

questions.text: 🗣️ (jbtiq_ml Q39 · S12 Time Series) "Why does ordinary K-fold CV lie for time series, and what does honest validation look like?
points: Random folds train on the future to predict the past — with autocorrelation, adjacent points are near-duplicates across folds, so the score measures interpolation, not forecasting. The inflation can be dramatic.
Second leak lives in features: rolling means, lags, or global normalizations computed over the full series before splitting carry future information into the past rows even under a correct split.

Honest scheme: walk-forward validation — train on an expanding (or rolling) window, test on the next block, step forward, aggregate across origins; add a gap/embargo between train and test when features have lookback windows. Rolling window when old regimes actively mislead.

Report performance per fold over time, not pooled — decay across folds reveals drift speed and dictates the retraining cadence; and compare against the naive baselines (last value, seasonal naive) that forecasting models embarrassingly often fail to beat.
Stationarity ties in: models assuming it (ARIMA-family) need differencing/transforms confirmed by ADF-style checks, and the validation must respect the same temporal discipline as the model.
questions.oneLiner: Random folds let the model train on the future and interpolate near-duplicates, so I validate walk-forward across multiple origins with an embargo for feature lookback — and any forecast that can't beat seasonal-naive isn't a model yet.

questions.text: 🗣️ (jbtiq_ml Q40 · S12 Time Series) "ARIMA, Prophet, or gradient boosting with lag features — how do you choose for a real forecasting problem?
points: ARIMA/SARIMA: principled for a single, well-behaved series — explicit AR/MA structure on a stationarized series, interpretable orders (via ACF/PACF), proper prediction intervals. Cost: per-series care, stationarity work, weak with covariates and many series.

Prophet: decomposable trend + seasonality + holidays, robust to missing data and outliers, built for many business series with strong calendar effects and analysts who aren't statisticians. Cost: rigid functional form — it underperforms when dynamics aren't calendar-driven, and it's not a magic upgrade over naive baselines.

GBM with engineered features (lags, rolling stats, calendar, promotions, price): wins when exogenous drivers matter and you have many related series — one global model learns across them. Cost: you own the feature engineering, the temporal CV discipline, and recursive-vs-direct multi-step strategy; extrapolating a trend beyond seen range is a known tree weakness.

Decision shape: one series + structure → ARIMA-family; hundreds of calendar-driven series + speed → Prophet or seasonal-naive; drivers + cross-series signal → global GBM (today's default in industry forecasting competitions and platforms).
Always anchor on naive/seasonal-naive baselines and validate walk-forward — the number of production forecasting systems that don't beat seasonal-naive is the field's dirty secret.

questions.text: 🗣️ (jbtiq_ml Q41 · S13 Recommender Systems) "Collaborative filtering vs content-based vs matrix factorization — mechanisms and the cold-start story for each.
points: Content-based: match item features to a profile built from the user's own history — no other users needed. Handles new items natively (they have features), fails new users (no history) and over-specializes (filter bubble: more of the same).

Collaborative filtering (user- or item-based neighbourhoods): learns from the interaction matrix only — captures taste patterns content can't ("people who liked X…"), but fails both new users and new items (no interactions) and struggles with sparsity; item-based aged better (item similarities are more stable, cacheable).

Matrix factorization (SVD-style, ALS): decompose interactions into latent user/item factors — denser generalization from the same sparse matrix, the classical quality winner. ALS specifically fits the implicit-feedback formulation (confidence-weighted, no observed negatives). Same cold-start weakness as CF; hybrids bolt content features onto the factors.
Cold-start playbook: new user → onboarding signals, popularity/context priors, bandit exploration; new item → content features + exposure boost; the practical answer is always a hybrid.
Implicit vs explicit matters more than people say: clicks are confidence, not preference — absence isn't dislike — which changes loss, negatives sampling, and evaluation.

links.label: Collaborative Filtering — User Based, Item Based

questions.oneLiner: Content-based survives new items but bubbles, CF learns taste but dies on cold start, matrix factorization generalizes the interaction matrix best — so production systems are hybrids, with implicit feedback treated as confidence rather than preference.

questions.text: 🗣️ (jbtiq_ml Q45 · S14 ML Systems & Architecture) "Fraud team wants a model. Walk me through build vs buy vs fine-tune — and the cost-of-error analysis that anchors it.
points: Anchor on the cost matrix first: a missed fraud costs the loss amount; a false positive costs a blocked customer and support load. Those two numbers set the operating point, the review-queue budget, and the accuracy bar any option must clear — decisions before models.

Buy when fraud isn't your differentiator and vendors have network effects you can't replicate (cross-merchant fraud signals) — evaluate on your data with a backtest, not their marketing metrics, and price the integration + per-transaction cost against your loss rate.

Build when your fraud patterns are proprietary, data volume is sufficient, and the economics at your scale beat vendor pricing — cost the full lifecycle (team, serving, monitoring, retraining, compliance), not the notebook.

Hybrid is the usual answer: vendor score as one feature inside your own model plus a rules layer for known patterns and instant response — you keep control of the operating point and the vendor hedges your cold start.

Governance rider: fraud models face adversarial drift (fraudsters adapt to whatever you deploy) — whoever supplies the model, you own the monitoring, the retraining cadence, and the human-review loop. That ongoing cost usually decides the question.

questions.text: 🗣️ (jbtiq_dl Q2 · S0 Math / DL Foundations) "Your softmax layer starts returning NaN once logits get large. What's happening mathematically, and what's the standard fix?
points: exp() of a large logit overflows float range → inf/inf → NaN; very negative logits underflow to 0 and can make the denominator collapse.
Softmax is shift-invariant: subtracting any constant from all logits changes nothing. So subtract max(logits) first — largest exponent becomes exp(0)=1, everything is safe.
Same idea generalizes to the log-sum-exp trick for log-probabilities; in practice you use fused log_softmax / cross-entropy kernels that do it internally instead of composing log(softmax(x)).
Senior link: this exact numeric pressure reappears in attention at long context (many logits, growing magnitudes) — why kernels compute softmax with running max/sum.
questions.oneLiner: Softmax is shift-invariant, so you subtract the max logit before exponentiating — log-sum-exp is the same trick in log space, and every serious kernel does it for you.

questions.text: 🗣️ (jbtiq_dl Q3 · S1 Foundations) "Why does a neural net need nonlinear activations at all — and how do you actually pick one today?
points: Without nonlinearity, any stack of linear layers collapses to a single linear map — depth buys nothing.
Sigmoid/tanh saturate: derivative ≈ 0 at the tails → vanishing gradients in deep stacks. Keep sigmoid for gates and output probabilities only.
ReLU is the cheap default: no saturation for positive inputs, sparsity — but dead units (stuck at 0 with zero gradient) under bad init/LR.
GELU/SiLU are the transformer-era default: smooth, small negative leak, empirically better at scale.
Rule: hidden layers → ReLU-family/GELU; output layer → dictated by the task (linear for regression, sigmoid/softmax for probabilities).
questions.oneLiner: Nonlinearity is what makes depth mean anything — hidden layers get ReLU or GELU, the output layer is chosen by the loss, and sigmoid in hidden layers is a vanishing-gradient bug.

questions.text: 🗣️ (jbtiq_dl Q6 · S1 Foundations) "What actually is an embedding — and why not just one-hot vectors?
points: A learned dense vector: row of a matrix, selected by token id, trained by backprop like any other weight — nothing mystical, it's a lookup table with gradients.
The geometry becomes meaningful because training pushes tokens used in similar contexts together — similarity = usefulness for the same predictions.
One-hot vectors are orthogonal and equidistant: no shared statistical strength between related tokens, and dimensionality = vocabulary size.
Upstream, tokenization (BPE-style subwords) decides the units: bounded vocab, no true OOV, at the cost of splitting rare words.
Trivia that lands: input embeddings and the output softmax matrix are sometimes weight-tied.
questions.oneLiner: An embedding is a trainable lookup row whose geometry is shaped by the loss — unlike one-hot, related tokens share statistical strength in a space that doesn't scale with vocabulary.

questions.text: 🗣️ (jbtiq_dl Q7 · S1 Foundations) "The universal approximation theorem says one hidden layer is enough. So why is everything deep?
points: UAT is an existence result: some wide-enough single hidden layer approximates any continuous function on a compact set. It says nothing about how wide, whether SGD finds it, or whether it generalizes.
The required width can grow exponentially in input dimension; depth buys compositionality — hierarchical functions expressed with exponentially fewer units when features build on features.
Depth is also an inductive bias: real data (language, vision) is compositional, so deep architectures match its structure and learn from less data.
Interview framing: approximation ≠ optimization ≠ generalization — UAT only addresses the first.
questions.oneLiner: UAT is an existence proof about approximation — depth wins on efficiency, learnability, and inductive bias, which are the three things the theorem is silent on.

questions.text: 🗣️ (jbtiq_dl Q9 · S2 Why Transformers Won) "LSTM in 60 seconds: what does each gate buy you?
points: The core trick is the cell state: an additive highway through time. Addition (not repeated matrix multiplication) is what lets gradients flow — the same insight residual connections reuse in space.
Forget gate: what fraction of the old cell state to keep. Input gate: what new information to write. Output gate: how much of the cell to expose as the hidden state.
GRU collapses this to two gates (update/reset), fewer parameters, usually comparable — the pragmatic default when you must use a recurrent model.
Honest limit: gating fixed vanishing, but not the sequential bottleneck — LSTMs still train one step at a time, which is why attention won anyway.
questions.oneLiner: The LSTM's additive cell state is a gradient highway, with forget/input/output gates controlling keep, write, and expose — it solved vanishing gradients but never solved sequential training.

questions.text: 🗣️ (jbtiq_dl Q10 · S2 Why Transformers Won) "Before transformers existed — what specific problem did attention originally solve in seq2seq, and how?
points: Vanilla seq2seq squeezes the whole source into one fixed-size vector — the information bottleneck; translation quality visibly degraded with sentence length.

Bahdanau attention: at each decoder step, compute a relevance score of the decoder state against every encoder state, softmax, and feed the weighted sum — content-based addressing over the source, alignment learned jointly with translation.
Luong simplified scoring (dot/general vs additive MLP) and the timing of where the context vector enters — worth naming to show you know the lineage.
The reframe that matters: attention began as a retrofit to fix RNN memory; the transformer's move was deleting the RNN and keeping only the retrofit.
questions.oneLiner: Attention was invented to break the fixed-vector bottleneck in seq2seq — a learned soft lookup over all encoder states per decoder step — and the transformer is what's left when you delete the RNN around it.

questions.text: 🗣️ (jbtiq_dl Q11 · S2 Why Transformers Won) "Give me the three real reasons transformers beat LSTMs — 'attention is all you need' is not an answer.
points: Parallelism: training computes all positions at once as dense matmuls — exactly what GPUs/TPUs are built for. The RNN's serial chain leaves the hardware idle.
O(1) path length between any two tokens, vs O(n) hops through a recurrent chain — credit assignment over long range stops decaying with distance.
Scaling economics: those two mean more tokens and parameters per dollar; transformers ride scaling laws that recurrent nets couldn't reach in practice.
The price: O(n²) attention cost in sequence length, and no built-in notion of order — positional information must be injected (Q15).

questions.oneLiner: Transformers won on parallel training, constant path length between tokens, and the scaling economics those unlock — paying for it with quadratic attention and the need for explicit positional encoding.

questions.text: 🗣️ (jbtiq_dl Q25 · S5 Training Mechanics) "Adam vs AdamW — what does each moment do mechanically, and why did 'decoupling' weight decay matter enough to rename the optimizer?
points: First moment: EMA of the gradient — momentum, smooths direction. Second moment: EMA of squared gradient — a per-parameter learning-rate scaler (big recent gradients → smaller steps). Bias correction fixes both EMAs' early-step underestimate.

Classic Adam + L2-in-the-loss: the decay term enters the gradient and gets divided by √v̂ — so weights with large gradient history get less decay. Regularization strength becomes entangled with gradient scale.
AdamW decouples: weight decay is applied directly to the weights at the update step, outside the adaptive machinery → decay means what it says. Default for transformer training.
Cost worth naming: two extra states per parameter → optimizer memory ≈ 2× model size in fp32 (this is a chunk of Q29's arithmetic).

links.label: Optimizer Family
links.target: 02-DL/05-Training Mechanics that make transformers work/01-Optimizer Family

questions.oneLiner: Adam steers with a gradient EMA and scales per-parameter steps with a squared-gradient EMA — AdamW pulls weight decay out of that adaptive denominator so regularization is uniform again, which is why it's the transformer default.

questions.text: 🗣️ (jbtiq_dl Q26 · S5 Training Mechanics) "Every transformer recipe starts with LR warmup. What actually goes wrong in the first thousand steps without it?
points: Early on, Adam's second-moment EMA is estimated from a handful of noisy gradients → the adaptive denominator is unreliable → some parameters take enormous effective steps.

The network itself is raw: attention distributions and output logits are unformed, gradients are large and poorly conditioned — a full-size LR at that moment produces divergence or saturation you may never recover from (original post-norm transformers were notoriously dependent on warmup; pre-norm reduced but didn't eliminate the need).
Warmup ramps the LR from ~0 over the first steps so statistics settle before full-size steps land; then a decay schedule (cosine/linear) takes over — large steps to traverse, small steps to converge.
Pair it in your answer with gradient clipping — warmup prevents early blowups, clipping insures against late ones (Q31, Q41).

links.label: LR Schedules & the Loss Landscape
links.target: 02-DL/05-Training Mechanics that make transformers work/02-LR Schedules & the Loss Landscape

questions.oneLiner: At step ten, Adam's adaptive denominator is noise and the network's distributions are unformed — warmup keeps steps tiny until both settle, then the decay schedule handles the rest of training.

questions.text: 🗣️ (jbtiq_dl Q28 · S5 Training Mechanics) "Modern LLMs use GELU or SwiGLU in the FFN instead of ReLU. What's actually better about them — and is anything worse?
points: ReLU: cheap, sparse, but a hard zero — dead units get no gradient, and the kink makes the loss surface less smooth.
GELU ≈ x·Φ(x): smooth, probabilistic gating by magnitude, small gradient for mildly negative inputs → fewer dead units, empirically better at transformer scale.

SwiGLU-class: the FFN becomes a gated product of two projections — a learned, input-dependent gate per hidden unit; consistently better quality per FLOP, standard in Llama-generation models (usually with the hidden dim trimmed to keep parameters comparable).
The honest downside: slightly more compute and (for gated FFNs) an extra projection matrix — negligible next to the matmuls, which is why everyone pays it.
Tie-in: activation choice interacts with init variance assumptions (He was derived for ReLU).

links.label: Activation Family
links.target: 02-DL/05-Training Mechanics that make transformers work/03-Activation Family

questions.oneLiner: GELU replaces ReLU's hard zero with smooth magnitude-gating so units can't fully die, and SwiGLU goes further by making the gate itself learned and input-dependent — better quality per FLOP for a rounding-error cost.

questions.text: 🗣️ (jbtiq_dl Q29 · S6 Training at Scale) "Rough out the training-memory budget for a 7B-parameter model with AdamW in mixed precision. Where does it all go?
points: Per parameter, mixed-precision AdamW keeps: bf16 weights (2B) + fp32 master weights (4B) + two fp32 Adam moments (8B) + gradients (2–4B) ≈ 16 bytes/param — the standard arithmetic from the ZeRO paper.
7B × 16B ≈ ~112 GB of state alone — already past a single 80 GB device before activations. That single sentence justifies the entire sharding industry.
Activations come on top, scaling with batch × sequence × depth × width — attacked with activation checkpointing (recompute in backward instead of store: memory for ~⅓ extra compute).
Contrast for effect: inference needs ~2 bytes/param (or less, quantized) + KV cache — training-vs-serving memory is nearly an order of magnitude apart.
This arithmetic is the why for ZeRO/FSDP (Q32): most of those 16 bytes are redundantly replicated across data-parallel ranks.

questions.text: 🗣️ (jbtiq_dl Q30 · S6 Training at Scale) "Mid-training in fp16 your loss goes NaN; the identical run in bf16 is fine. Explain the difference and where loss scaling fits.
points: fp16: more mantissa, but a narrow exponent range — small gradients underflow to zero, large intermediates overflow to inf → NaN cascades.

Loss scaling is the fp16 patch: multiply the loss (hence all gradients) by a large factor to shift them into representable range, unscale before the optimizer step; dynamic scaling backs off automatically when infs appear.
bf16: same exponent range as fp32 with less mantissa — no underflow drama, no loss scaling, drop-in; the default on modern accelerators. The lost precision is tolerable because SGD is noise-tolerant.
Both schemes keep fp32 master weights, and numerically touchy ops (softmax, norms, large reductions) typically run in fp32 regardless.

links.label: GPU Memory Budget & the Levers
links.target: 02-DL/06-Training at scale/00-GPU Memory Budget & the Levers

questions.oneLiner: fp16's narrow exponent range lets gradients underflow or overflow — loss scaling is the workaround — while bf16 keeps fp32's range with less mantissa, which is why it just works and became the default.

questions.text: 🗣️ (jbtiq_dl Q31 · S6 Training at Scale) "Your recipe calls for a batch of 4M tokens; your hardware fits an eighth of that. Separately, training occasionally hits a violent loss spike. Which two knobs, and how do they interact?
points: Gradient accumulation: run k micro-batches, accumulate gradients, step once — mathematically the large batch (average the loss correctly; safe in transformers since LayerNorm, unlike BatchNorm, has no cross-example statistics).

Gradient clipping (global-norm): if ‖g‖ exceeds a threshold, rescale — a cap on step size that turns a catastrophic batch into a survivable one. Insurance against rare spiky data (Q41's first responder).
The interaction: clip once, after full accumulation (and after unscaling any fp16 loss scale) — clipping each micro-batch clips a different quantity and changes the semantics.

Operational habit that reads senior: log the pre-clip gradient norm — it's the vital sign that tells you whether spikes are building or the clip threshold is doing daily work (a sign your LR is too hot).

links.label: GPU Memory Budget & the Levers
links.target: 02-DL/06-Training at scale/00-GPU Memory Budget & the Levers

questions.oneLiner: Accumulation buys the batch size memory won't, clipping caps the rare catastrophic step — and the clip must land once, on the fully accumulated unscaled gradient, or you're clipping something else entirely.

questions.text: 🗣️ (jbtiq_dl Q32 · S6 Training at Scale) "The model no longer fits on one GPU. Walk me up the parallelism ladder — data, tensor, pipeline — and where ZeRO/FSDP fits in.
points: Data parallel: replicate the model, split the batch, all-reduce gradients — scales throughput, but every rank holds the full 16 bytes/param (Q29). Dies when the model+state doesn't fit one device.

ZeRO/FSDP: still data parallel, but shard optimizer state, gradients, and finally parameters across ranks, gathering shards on demand — removes the replication without changing the math. The first thing to reach for.

Tensor parallel: split individual weight matrices across GPUs; activations sync inside every layer → needs NVLink-class interconnect, so keep it intra-node. For when a single layer is too big or too slow.
Pipeline parallel: assign contiguous layer blocks to stages; micro-batches keep stages busy, but the bubble (idle ramp-up/down) is the tax. For depth across nodes.
Real frontier training composes all three ("3D"); the design rule is: pick the cheapest parallelism that fixes what specifically doesn't fit.
questions.oneLiner: Data parallelism splits the batch, ZeRO/FSDP shards the redundant state, tensor parallelism splits the matmuls and demands fast interconnect, pipeline splits the depth and pays a bubble — you compose them by asking what exactly stopped fitting.

questions.text: 🗣️ (jbtiq_dl Q41 · S9 Diagnostics & Engineering Judgement) "Your loss spikes at step 40k and never recovers — triage it.
points: Look first: gradient-norm history around the spike (sudden wall vs slow build), and which layer produced the first inf/NaN — that split alone separates a data problem from a numerics problem.

Usual suspects: a bad data shard (corrupt/duplicated/adversarial batch — replay that exact batch to confirm); LR too hot for this phase or a schedule bug; fp16 numerics (Q30); and growing logits — attention or output logits drifting upward until softmax breaks (mitigations: z-loss, qk-layernorm).

Recover: restore a checkpoint from before the spike, skip or reshuffle the offending data window, resume with lower LR and/or tighter clipping — "never recovers" usually means the weights are poisoned, so rolling forward is throwing good compute after bad.
Prevent: checkpoint cadence sized to acceptable loss-of-work, deterministic data ordering so you can bisect to the batch, and pre-clip grad-norm dashboards as the early-warning signal.
questions.badge: Evergreen — the training-stability scenario every senior loop includes in some form.
questions.oneLiner: Check grad norms and the first NaN layer, suspect data shard, LR, fp16, or growing logits — then restore pre-spike, skip the offending window, and keep deterministic data order so the batch is bisectable next time.

questions.text: 🗣️ (jbtiq_dl Q42 · S9 Diagnostics & Engineering Judgement) "Offline eval says the model is great; production quality is clearly worse. Where do DL-specific train–serve skews hide?
points: Tokenizer/formatting mismatch is suspect #1 in the LLM era: chat template differences, special tokens, truncation side, padding — eval harness and serving stack silently disagree.
Numerics: trained bf16, served quantized (int8/int4/fp8) — your offline eval scored a different model than the one in prod. Re-run eval on the deployed artifact.
Sampling: eval greedy/fixed-seed vs production temperature/top-p, different max lengths and stop conditions — you measured a different decoding policy.
Distribution shift: real prompts don't look like the benchmark; plus mode flags (a dropout/norm-state bug class from Q27) surviving into a custom serving path.
The fix pattern: a golden set replayed through the production stack end-to-end as a release gate, plus sampled live-traffic re-evaluation.
questions.oneLiner: The model you evaluated is rarely the system you deployed — template and tokenizer drift, quantization, and sampling params all change the output distribution, so the only honest eval replays a golden set through the serving stack itself.

questions.text: 🗣️ (jbtiq_dl Q44 · S10 Adjacent Coverage) "Why do CNNs still beat vision transformers on small datasets — what's the inductive-bias story?
points: Convolution bakes in locality (nearby pixels relate) and translation equivariance via weight sharing — assumptions that are simply true of images, so the model doesn't spend data learning them.
A ViT has almost no spatial prior — patches plus positional encodings — so it must learn locality from data; with enough data that flexibility wins, with little data it loses to the CNN's head start.
This is the general law (echoes Q7): stronger inductive bias = better sample efficiency, lower ceiling; weaker bias = data-hungry, higher ceiling. Match the prior to the data budget.

Adjacent map to have ready in the same spirit: the generative lineage — AE → VAE → GAN → diffusion — each step fixing the predecessor's failure (no sampling → blurry samples → unstable training/mode collapse → stable but slow).
questions.oneLiner: Convolution hard-codes locality and translation equivariance, which are true of images — so CNNs win when data is scarce, and ViTs win once there's enough data to learn those priors and go beyond them.

questions.text: 🗣️ (jbtiq_dl Q45 · S11 Mechanistic Interpretability) "Users report the model consistently asserts one specific false fact. Beyond 'finetune it away' — how would you locate where that fact lives and reason about editing it?
points: Logit lens: project the residual stream at each layer onto the vocabulary — watch where in depth the wrong answer starts dominating; the fact's emergence is localized in layers, not diffuse.

Activation patching / causal tracing: run a clean and a corrupted prompt, swap activations component-by-component, and see which swap flips the output — a causal localization of the responsible layers/heads/MLPs.
Working picture: mid-layer MLPs act as key–value memories storing associations, while attention heads move information between positions — factual recall lives disproportionately in those MLPs.

Model editing (ROME-class) surgically rewrites the located MLP weights — impressive on the target fact, but brittle: side effects on related facts and paraphrases, so verify with a neighborhood eval, not a single prompt.

Two calibration caveats: raw attention maps are not explanations (weights ≠ causal importance), and superposition — features sharing neurons — is why current work leans on sparse autoencoders to get interpretable features at all.
questions.oneLiner: I'd localize with logit lens and activation patching — factual associations sit mostly in mid-layer MLP key–value memories — then treat ROME-style editing as surgery with side effects, verified on the fact's whole neighborhood, not one prompt.
